sq.ANSWER:
Adjacency Matrix: An adjacency matrix is a 2D array of size V × V (where V is the number of vertices), used to represent edges between vertices in a graph.

 Self-loops:

  • A self-loop is an edge that connects a vertex to itself.
  • In an adjacency matrix, a self-loop at vertex i is represented by a non-zero value at position A[i][i] (the diagonal elements).
  • If the graph is unweighted, this value is typically 1.

 Example of Self-loop:

Let’s consider a graph with 3 vertices and a self-loop at vertex 2:

Vertices: 0, 1, 2

Edge:  (2, 2) → self-loop at vertex 2

Adjacency Matrix:

Parallel Edges:

  • Parallel edges are multiple edges between the same pair of vertices.
  • An adjacency matrix does not naturally support parallel edges since it can only store a single value per vertex pair.
  • To represent parallel edges, you can store the count of edges between two vertices in the matrix (i.e., use a value >1).
  • Alternatively, adjacency lists are preferred for parallel edges.

Example of Parallel Edges:

Let’s say there are 2 edges between vertex 0 and vertex 1:

Edge: (0,1), (0,1)

sq.ANSWER:
Consider the Adjacency matrix

Graph

Edges Present:

  • (0, 1)
  • (0, 3)
  • (1, 2)
  • (2, 3)

This is an undirected graph with 4 vertices and 4 edges.

In an undirected graph, each edge is represented twice in the adjacency matrix — once at A[i][j] and once at A[j][i].

So, to count the total number of unique edges, we count all the 1s in the matrix and then divide by 2.

 Pseudocode:

Function countEdges(matrix, V):

    edgeCount = 0

    for i from 0 to V-1:

        for j from 0 to V-1:

            if matrix[i][j] == 1:

                edgeCount += 1

    return edgeCount / 2

Explanation:

  • The nested loop traverses the entire matrix.
  • For each 1 found (indicating an edge), we increment the edgeCount.
  • Since each edge appears twice, we divide the total count by 2 at the end.
sq.QUESTION_DESC: Write a function or pseudocode to count the number of edges in an undirected graph represented by an adjacency matrix.

lq.ANSWER:
Consider

Each student = node

A common project = edge between two students

Use adjacency matrix (2D array) to represent the graph

(a) Algorithm / Program to Implement Graph Using 2D Array

Pseudocode (Algorithm Style):

1. Start

2. Input total number of students: V (vertices)

3. Create a 2D array of size V x V, initialized to 0

4. Input total number of collaborations: E (edges)

5. Repeat E times:

    a. Input student IDs: u and v (where u and v are indices from 0 to V-1)

    b. Set adjacency_matrix[u][v] = 1

    c. For undirected graph, also set adjacency_matrix[v][u] = 1

6. Display the adjacency matrix

7. Stop

C- Program

#include <stdio.h>

#define MAX 100

int main() {

    int adj[MAX][MAX], students, edges;

    int i, j, u, v;

    printf("Enter number of students (vertices): ");

    scanf("%d", &students);

    // Initialize adjacency matrix

    for (i = 0; i < students; i++) {

        for (j = 0; j < students; j++) {

            adj[i][j] = 0;

        }

    }

 

    printf("Enter number of collaborations (edges): ");

    scanf("%d", &edges);

    for (i = 0; i < edges; i++) {

        printf("Enter pair of students who collaborated (u v): ");

        scanf("%d%d", &u, &v);

        adj[u][v] = 1;

        adj[v][u] = 1;  // Because collaboration is mutual (undirected)

    }

    // Display adjacency matrix

    printf("\nAdjacency Matrix:\n");

    for (i = 0; i < students; i++) {

        for (j = 0; j < students; j++) {

            printf("%d ", adj[i][j]);

        }

        printf("\n");

    }

    return 0;

}

Sample Input:

Enter number of collaborations (edges): 3

Enter pair of students who collaborated (u v): 0 1

Enter pair of students who collaborated (u v): 0 2

Enter pair of students who collaborated (u v): 1 3

(c) Inefficiency of Array-Based (Adjacency Matrix) Representation

Explanation:

An adjacency matrix uses a 2D array of size V × V, where V is the number of students (nodes). This causes space complexity = O(V²).

 Inefficiency in Sparse Graphs:

  • In most real-world scenarios, each student may collaborate with only a few others.
  • If there are 1000 students, the matrix will be 1000 × 1000 = 1,000,000 entries.
  • But if there are only 500 collaborations, most matrix entries will be 0, wasting space.

Why is this inefficient?

  • Memory is wasted storing zeros for non-existent connections.
  • Operations like iterating through neighbors of a node require scanning the entire row.
  • In contrast, an adjacency list stores only actual edges, making it more memory-efficient and faster for traversals.

When is adjacency matrix better?

  • When the graph is dense (many edges)
  • When you frequently need to check whether an edge exists between any two students — in O(1) time
